title: Profiling and Debugging Training Code
intro: Training that takes 9 hours instead of 2, or dies halfway through out of memory, is usually a code or data problem — not a hardware one. Measure before you buy bigger machines.

steps.prompt: Get a quick overview of the dataset: columns, types, null counts, and memory use.
steps.fake_output:
RangeIndex: 48210931 entries
 #  Column           Non-Null Count     Dtype
 0  amount           48210931 non-null  float64
 1  merchant_id      48210931 non-null  object
 2  country          31022004 non-null  object
memory usage: 11.3 GB
steps.explanation: merchant_id is stored as 'object' (Python strings) and 'country' has 17 million nulls.
steps.why: Converting low-cardinality string columns to 'category' dtype often cuts memory by 5-10x. The nulls matter too: if serving code fills missing country differently than training did, that's training/serving skew waiting to happen.

steps.prompt: Profile where training time actually goes, sorted by cumulative time.
steps.fake_output:
ncalls  cumtime  filename:lineno(function)
        1   6204.1  train.py:12(main)
  4810000   4890.7  features.py:44(compute_features)
     1200    980.2  model.py:30(fit_batch)
steps.explanation: 79% of the time is in compute_features — called 4.8 million times, once per row — not in the model at all.
steps.why: Per-row Python loops over data are the most common ML training bottleneck. Vectorizing compute_features with pandas/numpy operations typically makes it 50-100x faster — no GPU required.

steps.prompt: Profile memory line by line to find what's blowing up RAM.
steps.fake_output:
Line   Mem usage   Increment   Line Contents
  18    2210 MiB     0.0 MiB   df = load()
  19   13840 MiB  11630 MiB   df_all = pd.concat([df] * 5)
  20   25310 MiB  11470 MiB   features = df_all.copy()
steps.explanation: Two lines each add ~11GB — an unnecessary duplication and a full copy.
steps.why: Accidental copies are the classic cause of OOM-killed training jobs (exit code 137). Line-level memory profiling finds them in one run, instead of guessing.

steps.prompt: Convert the exploratory notebook into a plain Python script that can run in a pipeline.
steps.fake_output:
[NbConvertApp] Converting notebook notebook.ipynb to script
[NbConvertApp] Writing 8412 bytes to notebook.py
steps.explanation: Every code cell becomes part of a .py file, in order.
steps.why: Notebooks are great for exploration but terrible for production: cells run out of order, hidden state lingers. Converting is step one; refactoring into testable functions with a proper entry point is the real work.
